strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile question: whether SAM’s generalization gains can coexist with increased membership leakage. The reported single-query results provide an interesting empirical observation.
Experiments cover four image and tabular datasets, multiple attack types, and additional image-model architectures. The appendix supplies training hyperparameters and detailed attack results.

Analyzing performance by example influence is a useful perspective beyond aggregate accuracy. SharpReg is a simple optimization-based intervention that substantially reduces the evaluated attack accuracies, albeit with utility losses.
weaknesses: The central memorization explanation is not established. Section 3 evaluates SAM on buckets constructed from precomputed SGD influence scores; improved accuracy on these examples does not demonstrate increased memorization by SAM. There are no SAM-specific leave-one-out estimates or direct links between individual examples’ memorization changes and membership leakage. Differences in baseline difficulty and accuracy ceilings also complicate the bucket comparisons.

The proposed entropy metric has an unresolved definitional problem. Appendix C.1 assigns 2,153 test examples with entirely zero influence scores to the highest-entropy bucket, although Equation (3) has a zero normalization denominator for these examples. This convention needs justification and sensitivity analysis. More generally, normalized influence entropy measures concentration rather than the total amount of influence, so its interpretation as a memorization spectrum requires stronger validation.

The attack results contain consequential inconsistencies. Under balanced membership evaluation, Equation (8) and Table 4’s CIFAR-100 SGD train/test accuracies imply approximately 59.84% correctness-based attack accuracy, whereas Table 3 reports 77.04%. The manuscript does not explain weighting or sampling that would reconcile this discrepancy. Equation (12) also appears to have an incorrect sign in the modified-entropy definition. These may be reporting errors, but implementation verification is necessary before trusting the comparisons.

The privacy conclusion needs qualification. Table 1 shows SAM reducing multi-query attack accuracy on CIFAR-100 from 69.18% to 65.41% and on CIFAR-10 from 56.36% to 54.01%; Purchase-100’s single-query increase is only 0.29 percentage points, smaller than the reported standard deviations. Higher maximum accuracy among the tested attacks supports a narrower claim than generally increased leakage from flatter minima. SAM-radius sweeps, stronger likelihood-ratio attacks, and true-positive rates at low false-positive rates are missing.

SharpReg’s claimed separate anti-overfitting mechanism is inadequately supported. For the reported xi < 1, Equation (5) equals Equation (4) with lambda replaced by lambda/(1-xi), multiplied by 1-xi. Appendix C.4.1 acknowledges parameter redundancy, but the experiments do not disentangle this reparameterization and loss scaling from an independent regularization effect. Direct sharpness measurements and controlled optimization ablations are also absent.

The mitigation comparisons do not establish a compelling advantage. In Table 4, SELENA outperforms the selected SharpReg configuration on CIFAR-100 in both test accuracy (76.92% versus 76.14%) and single-query attack accuracy (55.15% versus 59.69%), and also achieves lower multi-query accuracy; it similarly dominates on Texas-100. SharpReg’s simplicity could justify a weaker tradeoff, but computational savings are not measured. Matched-utility comparisons against tuned early stopping and ordinary regularization are needed to establish the benefit of explicitly seeking sharper solutions.
